subject: Geography
description: Indian agriculture — Green Revolution, key crops + states, MSP, agricultural reforms, irrigation, food security, climate-smart agriculture.

questions.stem: GREEN REVOLUTION in INDIA started in which decade?

options.option_text: 1960s (peak in late 60s-early 70s)
1990s (after liberalization)
1980s (mid-decade onwards)
1950s (pre-independence era)

questions.explanation: GREEN REVOLUTION in INDIA: starts late 1960s. KEY ARCHITECT: M.S. SWAMINATHAN ('Father of Green Revolution in India', 1925-2023; Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan; first Indian to win World Food Prize 1987). KEY ELEMENTS: (1) HIGH-YIELDING VARIETY (HYV) seeds — wheat (NORMAN BORLAUG's IR-8 wheat dwarf varieties from CIMMYT, Mexico); rice (IR-8 from IRRI, Philippines). (2) IRRIGATION expansion — canals, tube-wells. (3) Chemical FERTILIZERS — N, P, K. (4) PESTICIDES + HERBICIDES. (5) MECHANIZATION — tractors, combines. (6) SUBSIDIES + price support (MSP). FOCUS REGIONS: PUNJAB, HARYANA, WESTERN UP — wheat. ANDHRA, TAMIL NADU, PUNJAB rice. RESULTS: (a) Food grain production: 1965 (~89 mt) → 1985 (~152 mt) → 2024 (~330 mt). (b) INDIA shifted from FOOD-IMPORT (PL-480 dependence) to FOOD-SURPLUS by 1970s. (c) Wheat production tripled by 1985. CRITICISMS: (i) Regional inequality (Punjab/Haryana booming; Bihar/eastern India lagging). (ii) Environmental degradation: groundwater depletion, soil salinity, pesticide pollution. (iii) Inequality: large farmers benefited more; small farmers debt. (iv) Monoculture, biodiversity loss. (v) High-input dependency. SECOND GREEN REVOLUTION (proposed): focus on RAINFED areas, eastern India, pulses + oilseeds + millets. EVERGREEN REVOLUTION (Swaminathan term): sustainable, climate-resilient agriculture. UPSC angle: GREEN REVOLUTION + sustainability tradeoffs in GS-3 economics + GS-3 environment. PYQ FREQUENCY: Green Revolution + Swaminathan in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: WHICH state is the LARGEST producer of WHEAT in INDIA?

options.option_text: Uttar Pradesh (~30% of national)
Punjab (with high productivity)
Haryana (smaller area)
Madhya Pradesh (a close 2nd)

questions.explanation: UTTAR PRADESH — LARGEST PRODUCER of wheat in India (~30%). PRODUCTIVITY-WISE PUNJAB has the highest wheat productivity (~5,500 kg/hectare vs UP's ~3,500 kg/ha) — hence PUNJAB is INDIA's TOP-PRODUCTIVITY agriculture state per area. WHEAT TOP STATES (rough share): (1) UP — ~30% national production. (2) MP — ~17%. (3) Punjab — ~16%. (4) Haryana — ~11%. (5) Rajasthan — ~10%. WHEAT BELT: Indo-Gangetic Plain (Punjab, Haryana, UP, MP). RICE TOP STATES: WB (~13%), Punjab (~10%), UP, AP, TN, Bihar. SUGARCANE TOP: UP (~50% — largest!), Maharashtra, Karnataka. COTTON TOP: Maharashtra (~25%), Gujarat (~24%), Telangana, AP. PULSES TOP: MP (~25%), Rajasthan, Maharashtra. OILSEEDS: MP, Rajasthan, Maharashtra (groundnut, mustard, soybean). MILLETS (Bajra, Jowar, Ragi): Karnataka, Rajasthan, Maharashtra. FRUITS: TOP banana = TN; TOP mango = UP; TOP grapes = MH; TOP apple = HP/J&K. SPICES: TOP tea = Assam (~50%) + WB; TOP coffee = Karnataka (~70%); TOP black pepper = Kerala. INDIA RANKS GLOBALLY: 2nd in WHEAT (after China), 2nd in RICE (after China), 1st in MILK (since 1998 — Operation Flood, Verghese Kurien), 1st in PULSES, 2nd in SUGARCANE (after Brazil), 1st in MANGO, 2nd in TEA. UPSC angle: agricultural geography + regional economic patterns. PYQ FREQUENCY: top crop-state pairings in SSC, UPSC, NDA 2-3× per cycle.

questions.stem: MSP (MINIMUM SUPPORT PRICE) is announced by:

options.option_text: Government of India based on CACP
RBI on banking interest rates
World Trade Organization (WTO)
State assemblies independently

questions.explanation: MINIMUM SUPPORT PRICE (MSP): price GUARANTEED by GOI to farmers; Govt commits to PURCHASE crops at MSP if market price falls below. AIM: protect farmers from market collapses; ensure remunerative prices. RECOMMENDATION: by COMMISSION FOR AGRICULTURAL COSTS AND PRICES (CACP) — set up 1965 under Min of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare. ANNOUNCED: by GOI based on CACP recommendation (often slight upward adjustment). MSP COVERS 23 CROPS (since 2018-19): (1) 7 CEREALS — paddy, wheat, jowar, bajra, maize, ragi, barley. (2) 5 PULSES — tur (arhar), moong, urad, gram, lentil. (3) 7 OILSEEDS — groundnut, sunflower, soybean, sesame, niger, safflower, rapeseed-mustard. (4) 4 COMMERCIAL — cotton, copra, jute, sugarcane (FRP for sugarcane — different from MSP). MSP CALCULATION FACTORS: (a) Cost A2 (paid-out costs only). (b) Cost A2+FL (Family Labour). (c) Cost C2 (comprehensive cost incl. imputed values). M.S. SWAMINATHAN COMMITTEE (2004-2006) — recommended MSP = C2 × 1.5 (50% profit margin). MODI GOVT (2018) committed MSP = A2+FL × 1.5 (less than Swaminathan). KEY INSTITUTIONS: (1) FCI (Food Corporation of India) — main procurement agency. (2) NAFED (National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation) — pulses, oilseeds. (3) Cotton Corporation of India — cotton. UPSC angle: 2020-21 FARM LAWS + farmer protests; MSP legalization debate ongoing. KEY: MSP is NOT a legal right; only an administrative announcement. PYQ FREQUENCY: MSP basics in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: WHITE REVOLUTION in INDIA refers to the dramatic increase in:

options.option_text: Milk production (Operation Flood)
Egg production (poultry sector)
Cotton production fabric quality
Pearl + diamond gem production

questions.explanation: WHITE REVOLUTION ('OPERATION FLOOD') — programme launched 1970 by VERGHESE KURIEN (1921-2012, 'FATHER OF WHITE REVOLUTION'); transformed India from MILK-DEFICIT country to LARGEST MILK-PRODUCER in the world (since 1998). PROGRAMME: developed COOPERATIVE-DAIRY MODEL — farmers organized in village cooperatives → district cooperatives → state cooperatives → national federation (NDDB — National Dairy Development Board). KEY: AMUL (Anand Milk Union Limited) in Gujarat — pioneer cooperative; founder TRIBHUVANDAS PATEL + Verghese Kurien. NUMBERS: India's milk production: 1950 ~17 mt → 1970 ~21 mt (Operation Flood begins) → 2024 ~230 mt (largest globally; ~22% of world output). AMUL pattern replicated as Mother Dairy (Delhi), Vijaya (AP), Aavin (TN), Nandini (Karnataka), etc. KEY INSTITUTION: National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) — set up 1965 by KURIEN; HQ in Anand, Gujarat. OTHER 'COLOR REVOLUTIONS' in Indian agriculture (memorize): (1) GREEN — food grains (Swaminathan). (2) WHITE — milk (Kurien). (3) YELLOW — oilseeds (1986 onwards; Technology Mission on Oilseeds). (4) BLUE — fish/aquaculture. (5) PINK — onion + meat/poultry. (6) ROUND — potato. (7) GOLDEN — fruits/horticulture. (8) RED — meat + tomato. (9) GREY — wool + fertilizer. (10) RAINBOW — sustainable agriculture combining several. UPSC angle: agricultural diversity + Verghese Kurien (PADMA VIBHUSHAN, World Food Prize 1989). PYQ FREQUENCY: White Revolution + Kurien in UPSC, SSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: KHARIF crops are sown in which season?

options.option_text: Monsoon (June-July, harvest Sep-Oct)
Winter (October-November sowing)
Summer (March-April sowing)
Pre-monsoon (April-May only)

questions.explanation: KHARIF (खरीफ) season — SOWN at start of MONSOON (June-July); HARVESTED in autumn (September-October). 'Kharif' means autumn (Arabic origin). KHARIF CROPS need: (a) HEAT + plenty of WATER (during growing). (b) Examples: RICE, MAIZE, COTTON, SOYBEAN, GROUNDNUT, JOWAR, BAJRA, RAGI, PULSES (MOONG, URAD, ARHAR), JUTE, SUGARCANE. RABI (रबी) season — SOWN in WINTER (October-November); HARVESTED in SPRING (March-April). 'Rabi' means spring. RABI CROPS need: (a) Cool growing season + warm to ripen. (b) Examples: WHEAT, BARLEY, MUSTARD, GRAM, PEAS, OATS, LENTILS. ZAID — minor third season; March-June (between Rabi harvest + Kharif sowing). Crops: WATERMELON, CUCUMBER, MUSKMELON, FODDER, MOONG (some). KEY INSIGHT: India's TWO MAIN crop seasons (Kharif + Rabi) ride the MONSOON cycle. SOUTHWEST MONSOON (June-September) brings ~75% of annual rainfall — drives Kharif. Northeast Monsoon (Oct-Dec, mainly Tamil Nadu coast) — secondary. KHARIF FAILURES — common in DROUGHT YEARS (2002, 2009, 2014); cause distress + farmer suicides. RABI more reliable due to assured irrigation in major belts. UPSC angle: AGRO-CLIMATIC zones + crop calendar; agriculture insurance schemes (PMFBY — Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana). PYQ FREQUENCY: Kharif vs Rabi in SSC, UPSC, NDA 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which is the LARGEST source of IRRIGATION in INDIA today?

options.option_text: Tubewells / groundwater (~60%)
Canal irrigation (about 25%)
Tanks (with declining share)
Rainwater harvesting only

questions.explanation: TUBEWELLS / GROUNDWATER — LARGEST source of irrigation in India today: ~60% of irrigated area. SHIFT HISTORY: in 1950, CANALS were dominant (~40%) + TANKS (~20%); GROUNDWATER (~30%). By 2020: GROUNDWATER (~60%) + canals (~25%) + tanks (~5%) + others (~10%). REASONS for groundwater dominance: (1) Subsidized electricity for tubewell pumps (especially Punjab, Haryana, UP, AP, Karnataka). (2) Canal water unreliable in many areas. (3) Easier to install than canal infrastructure. (4) Farmer-controlled. PROBLEM — GROUNDWATER DEPLETION: India is the LARGEST GROUNDWATER USER globally (~25% of world's extraction!). Punjab, Haryana, Western UP — STAGE-IV depletion (Central Ground Water Board classification — over-exploited). Some areas: water table dropping ~1 m/year. CONSEQUENCES: drying wells, requiring deeper drilling, energy costs rising, soil salinization. SOLUTIONS proposed: (a) MICRO-IRRIGATION (drip + sprinkler) — used in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, AP. (b) PRADHAN MANTRI KRISHI SINCHAYEE YOJANA (PMKSY, 2015) — 'Per Drop More Crop'. (c) Rainwater harvesting MANDATORY in some states. (d) Crop diversification — shift from water-intensive (rice, sugarcane) to less water-intensive (millets, pulses). NATIONAL WATER POLICY: 2002, revised 2012; emphasizes integrated water management. UPSC angle: water security, food-water nexus, climate change. PYQ FREQUENCY: irrigation sources in UPSC, SSC, geography 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: PM-KISAN (since 2019) provides INCOME SUPPORT to landholding farmers of:

options.option_text: ₹6,000 per year (in 3 installments)
₹2,000 per year (under-estimate)
₹12,000 per year (over-estimate)
₹20,000 per year (much over)

questions.explanation: PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) — Direct Income Support scheme launched 24 February 2019; effective from 1 December 2018. AMOUNT: ₹6,000 per year per landholding farmer family, paid in THREE INSTALLMENTS of ₹2,000 each (April-July, Aug-Nov, Dec-March). KEY INSTALLMENTS to date: ~17-18 installments released by April 2025; total ~₹3 lakh crore disbursed. ELIGIBILITY: ALL LANDHOLDING FARMERS, including SMALL + MARGINAL (initial 2018 design was only SMALL+MARGINAL; expanded in 2019). EXCLUSIONS: (1) Constitutional post holders (current/former). (2) Senior bureaucrats (Group A + Group B). (3) Income tax payers. (4) Central/state govt employees (sections of). (5) Pensioners with monthly pension > ₹10,000. (6) Professionals (doctors, lawyers, etc.). KEY: payment via DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) to bank accounts; AADHAAR-linked for transparency. NUMBERS as of 2024-25: ~9.7 crore farmers benefited; major reach. CONTRAST WITH OTHER SCHEMES: (1) PRADHAN MANTRI FASAL BIMA YOJANA (PMFBY, 2016) — crop insurance, partially subsidized premium. (2) PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana) — irrigation. (3) E-NAM (electronic National Agricultural Market) — online unified market. (4) SOIL HEALTH CARD scheme. (5) NATIONAL MISSION ON SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE. CRITICISM: ₹6,000/yr is INSUFFICIENT for distress; should be expanded; AGRARIAN CRISIS (farmer suicides) continues. STATES like TELANGANA had RYTHU BANDHU before PM-KISAN. UPSC angle: agricultural income support + welfare schemes. PYQ FREQUENCY: PM-KISAN in UPSC, MPSC current affairs 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The 'Blue Revolution' launched in India primarily aimed at increasing the production of which sector?

options.option_text: Increase in wheat and rice production volumes
Increase in fish and aquaculture production
Increase in sugarcane and sugar output levels
Increase in edible oilseed cultivation areas

questions.explanation: B is correct because the Blue Revolution (Neel Kranti) refers to the rapid growth in fish production and aquaculture in India. Option A (wheat/rice) relates to the Green Revolution, and Option C (sugarcane) has no associated colour-revolution tag in official policy.

questions.stem: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was established primarily to perform which function?

options.option_text: RBI, which manages monetary policy and banking supervision
Refinance agricultural credit and promote rural development
SIDBI, focused on financing small and medium enterprises
NHB, which provides refinance for housing loan portfolios

questions.explanation: B is correct: NABARD was set up in 1982 on the recommendations of the Shivaraman Committee to act as an apex institution for agricultural and rural credit refinancing. Options A, C, D describe RBI, SIDBI, and NHB respectively — each serves a distinct financing segment.

questions.stem: Which Indian state contributes the largest share of India's total tea production, accounting for roughly half the national output?

options.option_text: West Bengal, known mainly for Darjeeling tea gardens
Assam, contributing over 50% of India's total tea output
Tamil Nadu, home to the scenic Nilgiri tea estates
Kerala, known for high-altitude Munnar tea plantations

questions.explanation: B is correct: Assam produces about 52–55% of India's tea. West Bengal (Darjeeling) is famous for premium GI-tagged tea but contributes a far smaller volume. Tamil Nadu's Nilgiris and Kerala's Munnar are significant but secondary producers in volume terms.

questions.stem: The concept of 'Evergreen Revolution' — sustaining productivity gains without ecological damage — in Indian agriculture is most closely associated with which scientist?

options.option_text: Norman Borlaug, who developed high-yield wheat varieties
M.S. Swaminathan, advocating ecologically sustainable output
Verghese Kurien, who transformed India's dairy cooperative
C. Subramaniam, credited with India's first Green Revolution

questions.explanation: B is correct: M.S. Swaminathan coined 'Evergreen Revolution' to describe productivity growth that preserves soil health, water tables, and biodiversity. Norman Borlaug introduced HYV seeds (Green Revolution); Verghese Kurien led the White Revolution (Operation Flood); C. Subramaniam was the key policy architect behind the Green Revolution push in the 1960s.

questions.stem: Which fibre crop is popularly called the 'Golden Fibre' of India and is primarily cultivated in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta region?

options.option_text: Cotton, grown mainly in Maharashtra and Gujarat states
Jute, cultivated mainly in West Bengal and Assam delta belt
Silk, produced in Karnataka and parts of Northeast India
Flax, used primarily for linen fabric and linseed oil

questions.explanation: B is correct: Jute is called 'Golden Fibre' because of its golden-brown colour and high economic value; India is the world's largest producer, concentrated in West Bengal and Assam. Cotton is 'White Gold', silk is sometimes called 'Queen of Textiles', and flax is negligible in Indian cultivation.

questions.stem: The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY, 2016) was introduced to replace which earlier crop insurance arrangement that suffered from low farmer enrolment and delayed claims?

options.option_text: Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme introduced in 1985
National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) started 1999
Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana linked to farm households
Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana for irrigation cover

questions.explanation: B is correct: PMFBY (launched January 2016) superseded the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS, 1999) and its modified variant (MNAIS), which had low coverage and slow actuarial settlements. CCIS (1985) was an even earlier scheme. Option C is a health insurance scheme; Option D is an irrigation scheme — both unrelated to crop insurance.

questions.stem: Shifting cultivation is known by different local names across India. Which term correctly identifies the form practised by tribal communities in the northeastern hill states?

options.option_text: Bewar, the slash-and-burn method practiced in MP forests
Jhum, the rotational forest-plot clearing of the Northeast
Podu, practiced by tribal communities of Andhra Pradesh
Kumari, used by hill tribes of the Western Ghats region

questions.explanation: B is correct: Jhum (or Jhuming) is the specific regional name for shifting cultivation in Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram and other northeastern states. Bewar is used in Madhya Pradesh; Podu in Andhra Pradesh/Odisha tribal belts; Kumari in the Western Ghats. Examiners frequently test these regional synonyms to catch candidates who know only the generic term.
